title: Northern Plains: Bhabar, Terai, Bhangar and Khadar

cards.h: India's food bowl has an internal order
cards.b: The northern plains cover about 7 lakh sq km and feed hundreds of millions. They are not uniform. They vary in soil, drainage and flood risk from the foothills to the river. UPSC often asks for the sequence and the contrast between old and new alluvium.

The plains are made of alluvium from the Himalayan rivers, laid in a deep trough (a foredeep) formed in front of the rising Himalaya. Depth of deposits is thousands of metres in places. The plains extend about 3,200 km from the Indus delta to the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta.

A narrow belt, 8-16 km wide, along the foot of the Shiwalik. Rivers drop pebbles and boulders here. The coarse deposit is so porous that streams sink and disappear. It suits large trees, not crops.

Marshy land with tall grass and wildlife, such as the Dudhwa and Pilibhit Terai, was drained in the 1950s to settle refugees and expand farming, and today it is a major rice and sugarcane belt of Uttar Pradesh.

South of the Bhabar, the lost streams re-emerge in a damp, marshy belt, 15-30 km wide. It was dense forest with wildlife, much now cleared for farming (sugarcane, rice, wheat in Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand). Malaria used to be a problem. Dudhwa and Corbett lie on this belt.

Older alluvium. It forms the higher terraces, beyond flood reach. Often dark with lime nodules called kankar. Soils are rich but less renewed. Found away from the river channels.

Khadar is typically light coloured, sandy loam. It lies along the river banks in the Ganga and Yamuna valleys. Farmers raise vegetables, melon and rice on it, and the yearly silt reduces the need for fertiliser.

Newer alluvium in the active floodplain. Fine silt, light-coloured, replenished by yearly floods. Very fertile and ideal for rice, jute, vegetables. Floods are the cost of fertility.

Compare the two for exam use. Bhangar soils are older, darker and clayey at times, but often poorer in plant nutrients. Khadar soils are fresher and finer. The contrast is a standard two-mark question.

• Age: Bhangar is older (Pleistocene), Khadar is newer (Holocene).
  • Position: higher terraces vs lower floodplain.
  • Fertility: lower in Bhangar, higher in Khadar.
  • Kankar: present in Bhangar, absent in Khadar.
  • Flooding: Bhangar is safe, Khadar floods often.

Also remember reh or kallar: salt-affected soils, common in Haryana and Uttar Pradesh.

Four sub-regions by rivers: Punjab plains (doabs between five rivers, mostly irrigated), Ganga plains (Haryana to West Bengal; includes the Ganga-Yamuna doab), Brahmaputra plains (Assam, with many river islands like Majuli) and Rajasthan plain, the Thar. Rainfall drops westward, from over 150 cm in the east to under 50 cm in the west.

The plains hold the Green Revolution core (Punjab, Haryana, west UP). Bihar's Kosi, called the 'Sorrow of Bihar', shifted course by about 120 km over two centuries and flooded severely in 2008 after the Kusaha breach. Groundwater depletion in Punjab and Haryana is a serious concern, as shown by NASA GRACE data in 2009.

Likely questions: 'Differentiate Bhangar and Khadar', 'Describe the physiographic features of the northern plains', 'Why are the plains densely populated?'

  • Use a cross-section from foothills to river: Bhabar, Terai, Bhangar, Khadar.
  • Give a one-line fact per zone.
  • Link soil and water to crop patterns and population density.

quiz.q: The belt where streams disappear is the?

quiz.w: It is a damp, marshy belt.

quiz.q: Nodules of lime in Bhangar are?
Majuli, a river island, lies in?
The Bhabar belt width is about?
quiz.w: It is narrow along the Shiwalik foot.

quiz.q: Salt-affected soils of the plains are called?

quiz.w: A trough filled by alluvium before the rising Himalaya.
